tei:titleStmt.tei:title: יום טוב של ק״ק קארפינטראס ל״ט בחדש ניסן
Poetic Additions for 9 Nisan, for when guards protected the Jews of Carpentras from an attempted pogrom — by Rabbi Mordecai Astruc (1682)

tei:div.tei:head: Poetic Additions for 9 Nisan, for when guards protected the Jews of Carpentras from an attempted pogrom — by Rabbi Mordecai Astruc (1682)

tei:l.tei:note: Piyyuṭ before Barkhu for the evening prayer:

tei:lg.tei:l: Lauding, honor, and greatness the redeemed ones give;
They will sing, hymn, tell the praises of the Cause.
Light and joy, happiness and honor, redeemed from death;
They will tell, they will praise the name of the Cause.
To the Living Deity, who lifts up the fallen, they cheer,
And go and enthrone and bless the Cause.

tei:l.tei:note: And finish the evening prayer as on a regular weekday, up until “Forever we have hoped in You”
and say the ‘Al haNissim originating from the complete sage Rabbi Eliyahu Karmi of blessed memory in the year 5442,
whose mnemonic is he is in a pure state according to the abbreviated count.

tei:lg.tei:l: For the miracles and for the wonders
You showed us, burdened with troubles
On the ninth of the month of Nisan,
The year of “he is in a pure state”
Our thousandfold foes rose against us, without slack hands,
In rage and anger, to destroy us irrevocably,
from envy that came alongside hatred.
For the matter that we saw, the stress of our brother
Whose blood was spilled.
Vengeance-deity, Cause! Avenge your servants’ blood and forgive its land, its people!
And as we blood-redeemers rose up,
To come between judging and judging, blood and blood
Against the murderer.
Their hearts were boiling hot within them,
and they schemed schemes against us.
Grab the foxes for us, they would leave no gleanings!
And they took the sticks
to put this miniscule flock to the slaughter
in sorrow and grief.
They went out armed to kill mother and children alike,
to loot our loot, to pillage our houses.
The sound of bitter weeping, wailing and moaning,
in the middle of the highway
For we said “we are all lost! We’ve been decreed against!
Who will save us from the foes of men, the Cretan nation?
Outsiders and foreigners, all like wolves!
To cut down our remnant,
were it not for the Cause’s kindness, remembering the covenant
that was made at that time, and was our salvation.
For a commandment, when done, protects and saves.
And from Their holy abode the ruler’s spirit was angrily roused
For the Cause’s heart is in Their hand.
And They came to the gate to which they came.
And great was the Shepherd who removed them from our borders
and placed in our gates
guardians and soldiers —
each man with sword on thigh out of night-fear.
And the Cause overturned the schemes of the gentiles,
Saved us from death to life.
Not for us, Cause, not for us,
But rather in the merit of our ancestors
Did They not spurn us to destroy us or nullify our pact.
And due to the hand stretched out
We cannot bring thanksgiving or grain offering,
But rather song and laudation,
praise and hymns rather that slaughter, writhing and wailing.
And we established this day of happiness and joy.
It’s good to thank the Master of masters, giving to the poor.
Yours, Cause, is reign! You brought us from the vale of tears
and from darkness to light. You will build the Chosen House
where we will do our required offerings before You as of yore,
and thank Your great name forever.

tei:l.tei:note: And say the final Qaddish and Barkhu and ‘Aleinu etc.
For the morning service, say Zmirot for weekdays as usual until “And in your Torah...”
Reshut “The Living One God in whose hand is all” to the tune of Y’sod haKol
Muḥarrak “Go out, my soul, to the living God” to the tune of M’tziv Adama
From “the soul of all life” to “to You alone we thank.”

tei:lg.tei:l: The soul of a pure-hearted man there was who sought food for his home — ennoble You! —
A foe struck him with rebels’ lashes and killed him.
No man knew his grave!
The soul of Your congregation spread about hither and thither to know what became of him — immortalize You! —
and they found the murderer who had buried him in his tent.
Heaven exposes his iniquity, earth rises up against him!
The soul of he who chose death over life was unredeemed by the gentile allotment — designate You! —
and in his death they drowned him in the river since they found no redeemer.
These are the waters of strife, where the children of Israel strove.
The soul awaiting Your strong, courageous, and powerful liberation — enthrone You! —
on the enemy’s day was covered in dirt and stoned with stones.
Grab for us the foxes, the little foxes!
The soul pursued and stressed, inside and outside crushed — exalt You! —
on the day of making the murderer stand in judgment, he went out
for the innocent blood he had spilled earthward.
The soul of the covenant-blood They saw, and had mercy on Their people — distinguish You! —
and from Their heights aroused the ruler’s spirit upon them.
The heaven-dweller laughs; my Master mocks them!
The soul confined in her houses’ rooms, her eyes hanging on heaven — honor You! —
on the day they made guardians stand, their faces ashamed,
and they stood on guard three days.
The soul established a holiday to praise You, her heart thanking You — unify You! —
in place of weeping and moaning whose blood would be scattered to You,
in those days and at this time.
The soul of Your pious ones will hymn to You who stills the raging seas and their pounding — fortify You —
lighting candles in Your holy courts in the land of their captivity,
saying “And if our mouths were as full of song as the sea...” (verse)

tei:l.tei:note: And finish everything as on 15 Kislev, hallel and Torah reading.

tei:note.tei:p: In the siddur, this is preceded by the regular introduction to and text of the Barkhu written out.
In the Modim prayer, the final passage before an Al haNissim addition is inserted.

The word בׄתׄםׄ is marked with upper dots, because the poem was written in the year 5442, and the gematria of בׄתׄםׄ is 442, the short count for the year. This is reflected in the English with the bold letters HEIIAUESE, which has the sum of 8+5+9+9+1+300+5+100+5=442
Find previous note.. An additional note: in the Provencal dialect, word-final nasals merged to a velar eng sound, so Nisan and tam rhymed.
A hard to translate pun on Psalm 144:13’s “our thousandfold flocks” — with “our flocks” as tsonenu and “our foes” sonenu.
Zephaniah 2:5. Here used as an allegory for the Christian community.
These two lines largely derive from the festival additional service.

Referring to the final line before Yishtabaḥ. In the Provençal rite, as in the modern Italian rite, after the Song of the Sea was recited the piyyut Kol B’ruei, followed by the Shema’ as introduced by this line.
Both of these piyyutim were also recited on 15 Kislev in the Carpentras custom, and have thus already been transcribed. They can be found here.

The first two paragraphs of the Nishmat prayer. In the siddur these paragraphs are printed in full. The following text is a nishmat piyyut, recited (in this case) as an introdution to Ilu Finu and the rest of the Nishmat prayer.
See the note for “he is in a pure state”, spelled the same way.
We know the author of this piyyuṭ! It was written by R. Mordecai Astruc, who lived in the late 17th century and signed his name in a double acrostic.
i.e. A Jew was murdered by a gentile and buried in secret.
Printed is נִבְחַר, “will be chosen,” a printer’s error to make the text closer to Jeremiah 8:3 but which breaks the acrostic. Thanks to Yosef Razin for suggesting this emendation!
He was drowned for his crime.
A mob began to form, throwing rocks and dirt.
Printed is יָצָאתָה, “you went out,” a printer’s error which breaks the rhyme.
The rector of the Comtat sent forces to defend the Jews, which the poet credits to divine intervention.

In the Provençal dialect, intervocalic ד was pronounced /z/, so מוֹדֶה is a slant rhyme withיַזֶּה.. It’s not a full rhyme because ז itself was in the process of shifting to /v/. Provençal Hebrew was weird.
From the Al haNisim paragraph, as well as the She-’Asa Nisim blessing.

The double acrostic for this verse is of unclear meaning. It is marked as the two letters חס, which doesn’t fit with the rest of the piyyut’s אני מרדכי.. It can’t be an abbreviated form of last name Astruc, because he signs it elsewhere in piyyutim as אשטרוק.. And none of the common abbreviations for חׄסׄ make sense in context. Any ideas in the comments would be appreciated!
The poem before hallel and Torah reading, also recited on 15 Kislev, can be found here.
